nodes.name: Fixed-point subgroup H and generalized symmetric space Q
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ such that $\theta^m={\sf id}$. We then define the following two sets: \begin{align*} H &= G^\theta=\{g\in G\mid \theta(g)=g\}\\ Q &=\{g\in G\mid g=x\theta(x)^{-1} \mbox{ for some } x\in G\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: For an automorphism θ of finite order, H is the set of θ-fixed points and Q the set of elements xθ(x)^{-1}.

nodes.name: Generalized Symmetric Space
nodes.statement: The set $H$ is the fixed-point subgroup of $\theta$ and $Q$ is known as a {\em Generalized Symmetric Space}.

nodes.name: theta-twisted conjugation
nodes.statement: Both $G$ and $H$ act on $Q$ by $\theta$-twisted conjugation which we denote by $*$. For $g\in G$ and $q\in Q$ we have $$g*q=gq\theta(g)^{-1}.$$
nodes.statement_short: G and H act on Q by g*q = g q θ(g)^{-1}.

nodes.name: Twisted action restricted to H is conjugation
nodes.statement: Since $H$ is the set of fixed points, this action is simply conjugation when restricted to $H$.
assumptions: $H$ is the set of fixed points
conclusions: this action is simply conjugation when restricted to $H$

nodes.name: Q is isomorphic to G/H for involutions
nodes.statement: Also, if $\theta$ is an involution, then $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$.
conclusions: $Q\cong G/H$ under the map $\tau : G\to Q$ given by $\tau(g)=g\theta(g)^{-1}$

nodes.name: H-orbits on Q correspond to H-double cosets
nodes.statement: In particular, if $\theta$ is an involution it is known that $H\backslash Q\cong H\backslash G/H$.

nodes.name: Dihedral group D_n
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we denote by $D_n$ the group of symmetries of the regular $n$-gon. More specifically, $D_n$ is a finitely generated group given by the presentation $$D_n=\langle r,s\mid r^n=s^2=1,\ sr=r^{-1}s\rangle.$$
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
differentia: the group of symmetries of the regular $n$-gon
nodes.statement_short: D_n is the symmetry group of the regular n-gon, presented as <r,s | r^n=s^2=1, sr=r^{-1}s>.

nodes.name: Normal form in D_n
nodes.statement: From the presentation it is clear that \[ D_n = \{ 1, r, r^2, \ldots, r^{n-1}, s, rs, r^2s, \ldots, r^{n-1}s \} \] and we say that an element of $D_n$ is presented in \emph{normal form} if it is written as $r^ks^m$ for some integers $0 \le k < n$ and $s \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Every element of D_n is written uniquely as r^k s^m with 0<=k<n, m in {0,1}.

nodes.name: Z_n and its unit group U_n
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, $\mathbb{Z}_n$ denotes the additive group of integers modulo $n$ and $U_n$ denotes the multiplicative group of units of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Units of Z_n are the residues coprime to n
nodes.statement: Recall that $a \in U_n$ if and only if $(\dot{a},n) = 1$ for any representative integer $\dot{a}$ of $a \in \mathbb{Z}_n$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
conclusions: $a \in U_n$ if and only if $(\dot{a},n) = 1$ for any representative integer $\dot{a}$ of $a \in \mathbb{Z}_n$

nodes.name: k-th roots of unity in Z_n
nodes.statement: We also find it useful to have terminology for the $k$-th roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ (equivalently in $U_n$), which can be described by $$\mathcal{R}_n^k:=\{a\in U_n\mid a^k=1\}.$$
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Automorphism group of the dihedral group
nodes.statement: The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the group of affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}_n$: $$\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\cong \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)=\left\{ ax+b: \mathbb{Z}_n\to\mathbb{Z}_n \mid a \in U_n, b \in \mathbb{Z}_n \right\}$$ and the action of $ax+b$ on elements of $D_n$ in normal form is given by: \[ (ax+b).(r^k s^m) = r^{ak+bm}s^m.\]
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
conclusions: The automorphism group of $D_n$ is isomorphic to the group of affine linear transformations of $\mathbb{Z}_n$
nodes.statement_short: Aut(D_n) is the affine group Aff(Z_n) = {ax+b : a in U_n}, acting by r^k s^m -> r^{ak+bm} s^m.
nodes.label: lem:aut

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.1
nodes.statement: Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in U_n \}$. So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to $n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$. Putting these together, we see that if $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$. There is now a clear map from $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\to \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: An automorphism must send r to an element r^a of order n and s to a reflection r^b s; this gives the map to Aff(Z_n).

nodes.name: Images of the generators
nodes.statement: Observe that $\theta(r)$ must have order $n$ since $r$ does. The elements of $D_n$ of order $n$ are precisely the $\{ r^a \mid a \in U_n \}$. So let $\theta(r) = r^a$ for some $a$ relatively prime to $n$. Similarly, $\theta(s)=r^bs$ for some $0 \le b < n$ since $s$ has order 2 and the only elements of $D_n$ of order 2 are of the form $r^bs$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: θ(r)=r^a with a a unit and θ(s)=r^b s, by orders of elements.

nodes.name: Identify with Aff(Z_n)
nodes.statement: Putting these together, we see that if $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$, then for any $r^ks^m\in D_n$ we must have $\theta(r^ks^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m$. There is now a clear map from $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\to \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ and it is easily checked to be an isomorphism.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Combine to get θ(r^k s^m)=r^{ak+bm}s^m and the isomorphism to Aff(Z_n).

nodes.name: Affine notation theta = ax+b
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we abuse notation and write $\theta = ax+b$ for elements $\theta \in \operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ according to Lemma \ref{lem:aut}.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group

nodes.name: Inner automorphisms of D_n
nodes.statement: Consider $\theta = \operatorname{conj}(g)$, conjugation by an element $g\in D_n$. If $\theta = ax + b$ from Lemma \ref{lem:aut}, and if $g=r^k$, then it is easy to see that $a=1$ and $b=2k$ (in $U_n$ and $\mathbb{Z}_n$ respectively). Also, if $g=r^ks$, then we have $a=n-1$ and $b=2k$. In particular, if $\theta=ax+b$ is an \emph{inner automorphism}, then (abusing notation) we have $a\equiv\pm 1 \pmod{n}$. Also, we see that when $n$ is even, there are $n$ distinct inner automorphisms (corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$, and when $n$ is odd, there are $2n$ distinct inner automorphisms corresponding to $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{n}$ and $b\in\langle2\rangle=\mathbb{Z}_n$. Finally, note that the identity automorphism of $D_n$ corresponds to $x \in \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: Conjugation by r^k is x+2k and by r^k s is (n-1)x+2k; so inner automorphisms have a = ±1, n of them for n even and 2n for n odd.

nodes.name: Diagram automorphism of D_n
nodes.statement: It is well known from the theory of Coxeter groups that when $n$ is even, there is an outer automorphism of $D_n$ corresponding to the interchanging of the two conjugacy classes of reflections, also known as the diagram automorphism (cf. \cite[\S4.2]{Bourbaki}). This automorphism is described by $\theta=ax+b$ where $a=n-1$ and $b=n-1$. The previous example shows that this automorphism is inner when $n$ is odd, and outer when $n$ is even.
nodes.section: 1.1 The Dihedral Group and its Automorphism Group
nodes.statement_short: For n even, the diagram automorphism swapping the two reflection classes is (n-1)x+(n-1), which is outer.
nodes.label: coxeter-example

nodes.name: ZDiv(c)
nodes.statement: For any $c\in\mathbb{Z}_n$, we define $\zdiv{c}=\{y\in\mathbb{Z}_n\mid cy\equiv 0 \mbox{ mod } n\}$.

nodes.name: ZDiv(c) is a subgroup
nodes.statement: It is trivial to check that $\zdiv{c}$ is a subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.

nodes.name: Proof that |ZDiv(c)| = gcd(c,n)
nodes.statement: In particular, $\zdiv{c}=\operatorname{ker}\pi_{c}$ where $\pi_{c}:\mathbb{Z}_n\to\mathbb{Z}_n$ given by $\pi_{c}(x)=cx$. Note that $\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})=\langle c\rangle$ and so $|\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})|=\frac{n}{\gcd(c,n)}$.
nodes.statement_short: ZDiv(c) is the kernel of multiplication by c, whose image <c> has order n/gcd(c,n).

nodes.name: Order of ZDiv(c)
nodes.statement: Since $\operatorname{im}(\pi_{c})\cong \mathbb{Z}_n/\operatorname{ker}(\pi_{c})\cong \mathbb{Z}_n/\zdiv{c}$, it follows that $|\zdiv{c}|=\gcd(c,n)$.

nodes.name: Automorphisms of order dividing k
nodes.statement: Let $k\geq 1$ be an integer and $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ with $\theta=ax+b$. Then $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
conclusions: $\theta^k={\sf id}$ if and only if $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $b\in \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$
nodes.statement_short: θ=ax+b has θ^k=id iff a is a k-th root of unity and b is killed by 1+a+...+a^{k-1}.
nodes.label: prop:orderk

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.1
nodes.statement: Straightforward computation in $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ gives us that $$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$ Since we have identified the identity automorphism with $x \in \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ the following two equations hold: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation} In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ $b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute θ^k = a^k x + (1+a+...+a^{k-1})b and compare with the identity x.

nodes.name: Congruences for theta^k = id
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: congruences

nodes.name: Compute theta^k
nodes.statement: Straightforward computation in $\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ gives us that $$\theta^k=a^kx+(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)b$$
nodes.statement_short: Compute the k-th power of ax+b.

nodes.name: Compare with identity
nodes.statement: Since we have identified the identity automorphism with $x \in \operatorname{Aff}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ the following two equations hold: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} a^k & \equiv 1 \pmod{n} \\ (a^{k-1} + a^{k-2} + \cdots + 1) b & \equiv 0 \pmod{n}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Equate with the identity x to get the two congruences.

nodes.name: Translate into notation
nodes.statement: In the notation described above, these are evidently equivalent to $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and\\ $b\in~\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The congruences say a is in R_n^k and b in ZDiv(1+...+a^{k-1}).

nodes.name: Aut_k(D_n)
nodes.statement: In what follows, we let $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)=\{\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n) \mid \theta^k={\sf id}\}\subseteq \operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$.

nodes.name: Number of automorphisms of order dividing k
nodes.statement: For any $n$ and $k\geq 1$, we have $$|\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)|=\sum_{a\in \mathcal{R}_n^k}\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n).$$
nodes.statement_short: |Aut_k(D_n)| is the sum over k-th roots of unity a of gcd(1+a+...+a^{k-1}, n).
nodes.label: prop:numauts

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement: This follows from Proposition \ref{prop:orderk}: for any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ there are $$\abs{\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1}}=\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1,n)$$ elements $b$ such that $(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+1)b\equiv 0$ (mod $n$), and every automorphism $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ must be of this form.
nodes.statement_short: Count, for each a, the b allowed by Proposition 2.1: |ZDiv(1+...+a^{k-1})| = gcd(1+...+a^{k-1}, n).

nodes.name: Equivalence of automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1, \theta_2\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$. We say that $\theta_1$ is \textit{equivalent} to $\theta_2$ and write $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if they are conjugate to each other, i.e. if there is $\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ with $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$. For any $\theta\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ we let $\overline{\theta}=\{\sigma\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)\mid \theta\sim \sigma\}$ be the equivalence class of $\theta$.

nodes.name: Equivalence allows all automorphisms
nodes.statement: This definition of equivalence is broad (since we allow conjugation by any automorphism, not just the inner ones), but still useful. In particular, it simplifies the statement of the following proposition and it allows us not to worry about the parity of $n$ in several places.

nodes.name: Criterion for equivalence of automorphisms
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ and $\theta_2=cx+d\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$. Then $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ for some $f\in U_n$.
conclusions: $\theta_1\sim\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ for some $f\in U_n$
nodes.statement_short: ax+b ~ cx+d iff a=c and fb-d lies in <a-1> for some unit f.
nodes.label: prop:equivalence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\mathbb{Z}_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$ where $f^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ since $f\in U_n$. Then $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$. Thus, we can conclude that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-g(a-1)= d$. The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate ax+b by σ=fx+g explicitly to get ax+fb-g(a-1) and compare coefficients.

nodes.name: Conjugating automorphism and its inverse
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\sigma=fx+g\in\operatorname{Aut}(D_n)$ (so that $f\in U_n$ and $g\in\mathbb{Z}_n$). It is easily checked that $\sigma^{-1}=f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g$ where $f^{-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ since $f\in U_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Take σ=fx+g and compute its inverse.

nodes.name: Compute the conjugate
nodes.statement: Then $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\tau$, where $\tau=f(a(f^{-1}x-f^{-1}g)+b)+g=ax+fb-g(a-1)$.

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement: Thus, we can conclude that $\sigma\theta_1\sigma^{-1}=\theta_2$ if and only if $a=c$ and $fb-g(a-1)= d$. The second equation can be written as $fb-d=g(a-1)$, and thus $fb-d\in\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality with cx+d forces a=c and fb-d in <a-1>.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes of automorphisms of order dividing k
nodes.statement: Suppose $n$ is fixed and let $k\geq 1$. \begin{enumerate} \item For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}$. \item For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$. \item The set $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$ where $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$ and $B$ is an orbit of $U_n$ on \hbox{$\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$}. \end{enumerate}
conclusions: For any $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, $U_n$ acts on the cosets $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
The set $\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)$ is partitioned into equivalence classes indexed by pairs $(a,B)$
nodes.statement_short: Classes of Aut_k(D_n) are indexed by a in R_n^k and a U_n-orbit on ZDiv(1+...+a^{k-1})/<a-1>.
nodes.label: lem:equivalence

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$. For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1) from (a-1)(1+...+a^{k-1})=a^k-1; part (2) since U_n stabilizes subgroups; part (3) restates Proposition 2.5.

nodes.name: Part (1)
nodes.statement: Part (1) is trivial since $(a-1)(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1)=a^k-1\equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Part (2)
nodes.statement: For part (2), we simply recognize that $U_n=\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)$ acts on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ by multiplication and since every subgroup is cyclic, $U_n$ must stabilize the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: U_n = Aut(Z_n) stabilizes the cyclic subgroups of Z_n.

nodes.name: Part (3)
nodes.statement: Finally, part (3) is simply Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} in terms of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (3) is Proposition 2.5 rephrased via the U_n-action.

nodes.name: Number N_a of equivalence classes with leading coefficient a
nodes.statement: For fixed $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, we want to compute \begin{equation} N_a:=|\{\overline{\theta}\mid \theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)\}|. \end{equation}
also_stated_at: Recall that we denote the equivalence class of an involution $\theta$ by $\overline{\theta}$ and the number of equivalence classes with fixed leading coefficient $a$ by: \[ N_a:=\left|\left\{ \overline{\theta} \mid \theta = ax + b \in \operatorname{Aut}_2(D_n) \right\}\right|.\]

nodes.name: Definition of N_a
nodes.statement: N_a:=|\{\overline{\theta}\mid \theta=ax+b\in\operatorname{Aut}_k(D_n)\}|.
nodes.label: eq:numequiv

nodes.name: N_a counts U_n-orbits
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence}, given $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$, computing $N_a$ amounts to counting the number of orbits of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$.
conclusions: computing $N_a$ amounts to counting the number of orbits of the $U_n$-action on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$

nodes.name: Number of U_n-orbits on ZDiv/<a-1>
nodes.statement: Let $n$ be fixed and let $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^k$. Then, the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
conclusions: the number of orbits of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ is equal to the number of divisors of $$\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots+a+1,n)}{n}.$$
nodes.statement_short: The U_n-orbits on ZDiv(1+...+a^{k-1})/<a-1> are counted by the divisors of gcd(a-1,n)gcd(1+...+a^{k-1},n)/n.
nodes.label: unorbits

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.7
nodes.statement: The $U_n$-orbits on $\mathbb{Z}_n$ are indexed by the subgroups of $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Thus, the $U_n$-orbits on $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ are indexed by subgroups $L\leq \mathbb{Z}_n$ such that $\langle a-1\rangle\leq L\leq \zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$. It is well known that the subgroup lattice of $\mathbb{Z}_n$ is isomorphic to the divisor lattice of $n$. Under the previous lattice isomorphism, the subgroup $\langle a-1\rangle$ corresponds to the divisor $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and the subgroup $\zdiv{a^{k-1}+a^{k-2}+\cdots +a+1}$ corresponds to the divisor $$\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+1,n)},$$ and the subgroups between these groups correspond to the divisors of $n$ between $\gcd(a-1,n)$ and $\frac{n}{\gcd(a^{k-1}+\cdots+a+a,n)}$ in the divisor lattice. nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1

Therefore, for any $q\in Q $, we can find $g\in G$ such that $g1\theta(g)^{-1}=q$ and so $G*1=Q$. Hence $G\backslash Q=\{Q\}$.

nodes.name: Number of square roots of unity modulo n
nodes.statement: Suppose that $n\geq 1$ and $n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$ where the $p_i$ are distinct odd primes. Then, $$|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=\begin{cases} 2^k & \mbox{ if $m=0,1$}\\ 2^{k+1} & \mbox{ if $m=2$}\\ 2^{k+2} & \mbox{ if $m\geq 3$}. \end{cases}$$

nodes.name: Construction of square roots of unity
nodes.statement: We include the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:squareroots1} in Appendix \ref{sec:appendix} because it demonstrates exactly how to construct the square roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ provided we have the prime factorization of $n$. The construction only involves the Euclidean Algorithm and a map provided by the Chinese Remainder Theorem. One can use the procedure described in the proof to effectively compute the square roots of unity in $\mathbb{Z}_n$ for any $n$. The construction of the square roots of unity provided in the appendix also provides the understanding necessary for Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} below.

nodes.name: Reduction for classifying involutions
nodes.statement: Let $\theta_1 = ax+b$ and $\theta_2=cx+d$. We know from Proposition \ref{prop:equivalence} that if $\theta_1 \sim \theta_2$, then $a=c$. Thus, to determine the equivalence classes of involutions it suffices to fix an $a \in \mathcal{R}_n^2$ and determine when $ax+b \sim ax+d$. Furthermore, according to Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence}, with $a$ fixed, we simply need to describe the action of $U_n$ on $\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle$ in order to describe all the equivalence classes.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent involutions share a, so classes reduce to the U_n-action on ZDiv(a+1)/<a-1>.

nodes.name: Equivalence classes of involutions with fixed a
nodes.statement: Let $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$. The following hold. \begin{enumerate} \item $\langle a-1\rangle\leq \zdiv{a+1}$ and $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|\leq 2$. \item $N_a = \left| \zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle \right| \leq 2 $. \item $N_a=2$ if and only if $n=2^m\cdot k$ where $k\geq1$ is odd, $m > 0$, and \hbox{$a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.} \end{enumerate}
conclusions: $N_a=2$ if and only if $n=2^m\cdot k$ where $k\geq1$ is odd, $m > 0$, and \hbox{$a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.}

nodes.statement: The first part of (1) is simply a restatement of Proposition \ref{lem:equivalence} part (1). Now, suppose that $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1\rangle|=j$. It is well known that $|\langle a-1\rangle|=\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}$ and we have already observed that $|\zdiv{a+1}|=\gcd(a+1,n)$. Thus we have that $\frac{\gcd(a+1,n)}{\frac{n}{\gcd(a-1,n)}}=j$, or $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$. Now, suppose that $$n=2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}$$ with $m\geq 0$, the $p_i$ distinct odd primes, and $r_i\geq 1$. Then, we must have that \begin{itemize} \item[] $\gcd(a+1,n)=2^{m'}p_1^{s_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k}$ with $m'\leq m$ and $0\leq s_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$, and \item[] $\gcd(a-1,n)=2^{m''}p_1^{t_1}\cdots p_k^{t_k}$ with $m''\leq m$ and $0\leq t_i\leq r_i$ for all $i$. \end{itemize} Now, we note that for all $i\in\{1,...,k\}$ either $s_i=0$ or $t_i=0$. Indeed, if $s_i>0$ and $t_i>0$ then $p_i$ divides both $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible (since $p_i>2$). Similarly, either $m'\leq1$ or $m''\leq1$; otherwise, $2^{\min\{m',m''\}}$ divides $a-1$ and $a+1$ which is impossible. Since $\gcd(a+1,n)\gcd(a-1,n)=jn$, we have that $$2^{m'+m''}p_1^{s_1+t_1}\cdots p_k^{s_k+t_k}=j2^mp_1^{r_1}\cdots p_k^{r_k}.$$ Now, since for all $i$ either $t_i=0$ or $s_i=0$, we necessarily have $s_i+t_i=r_i$. Dividing out, we get $2^{m'+m''}=j2^m$. We also know that $m'\leq m$ and $m''\leq m$ and since either $m'\leq 1$ or $m''\leq 1$, we have $m\leq m'+m''\leq m+1$. Dividing out we have $j=2^{m'+m''-m}$ and so $1\leq j\leq 2$ as required. Now, according to Theorem \ref{unorbits}, $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $\frac{\gcd(a-1,n)\gcd(a+1,n)}{n}$, and thus $N_a$ is the number of divisors of $j$ computed above. Therefore, $N_a=1$ if $j=1$ and $N_a=2$ if $j=2$. In either case, $N_a = |\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle| \le 2$ proving Claim (2). Finally, according to the proof of (1), we have $j=2$ if and only if $m'=1$ and $m''=m$ or $m'=m$ and $m''=1$. In the first case, we have that $2^m$ divides $a-1$, and in the second case we have that $2^m$ divides $a+1$. Therefore, $a \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{2^m}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.6
nodes.statement: According to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, we know $N_a$ for every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$. When $m=0$, $n$ is odd and we know that $N_a=1$ for all $a$. Thus, there is one equivalence class for every element of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ proving the first formula. If $m=1,2$, then every $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$ is odd and so satisfies $a\equiv \pm 1\pmod{m}$. Thus for every element $a\in\mathcal{R}_n^2$, we get two equivalence classes for a total of $2\cdot|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ equivalence classes. Finally, when $m\geq 3$, using the construction of the elements of $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ found in the proof in the appendix, we see that exactly half of these elements satisfy the condition $a\equiv\pm 1\pmod{m}$. Therefore, for half the elements in $\mathcal{R}_n^2$ we have $N_a=1$ and for the other half we have $N_a=2$ giving us a total of $2^{k+2}+(2^{k+2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2^{k+2})=2^{k+3}-2^{k+1}$ equivalence classes, proving the result.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the power of 2 in n, summing N_a from Theorem 4.5 over the square roots of unity.

nodes.name: OEIS connection with groups of order 2n
nodes.statement: According to the Online Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences, the sequence described in Corollary \ref{cor:equivclassformula} also counts the number (up to isomorphism) of groups of order $2n$ that have a subgroup isomorphic to $\mathbb Z_n$ \cite{oeisA147848}. To be more precise, we include a brief discussion of the natural bijection between these two objects. Suppose $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution. Then $w_a:\mathbb{Z}_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbb{Z}_n)=U_n$ given by $w_a(0)=1$ and $w_a(1)=-a$ is an injective homomorphism and induces a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on $\mathbb{Z}_n$. Next, we define $f:\mathbb{Z}_2\times\mathbb{Z}_2\to\mathbb{Z}_n$ by $f(c,d)=0$ if $c=0$ or $d=0$ and $f(1,1)=b$; it is easily shown that $f$ is a 2-cocycle if and only if $b\in\zdiv{a+1}$. Finally, it is well known (see \cite[Chapter 6.6]{weibel})) that 2-cocyles give rise to group extensions and two different 2-cocycles give isomorphic group extensions if they are cohomologous. A simple calculation shows that if $\theta=ax+b$ and $\theta'=ax+b'$, then the corresponding 2-cocycles are cohomologous if and only if $b-b'\in\langle a-1\rangle$, which matches the characterization of automorphisms being equivalent above.
nodes.statement_short: C_n also counts groups of order 2n with a subgroup Z_n (OEIS A147848), via 2-cocycles b of the Z_2-action -a.

nodes.name: Twisted involutions R

nodes.name: Q is a subgroup for involutions
nodes.statement: If $\theta=ax+b$ is an involution, then $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and under the natural isomorphism $\psi: \langle r \rangle \buildrel\cong\over\longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_n$ we have \[ \psi(Q) = \begin{cases} \langle a-1 \rangle, & \text{if} \quad b \in \langle a-1 \rangle \\ \zdiv{a+1}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \] Furthermore, $R \setminus Q = \{r^k\mid k\in\zdiv{a+1}\setminus\langle a-1\rangle\}\cup\{r^ks \mid k(a-1)\equiv -b\pmod{n}\}$
conclusions: under the natural isomorphism $\psi: \langle r \rangle \buildrel\cong\over\longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}_n$ we have \[ \psi(Q) = \begin{cases} \langle a-1 \rangle, & \text{if} \quad b \in \langle a-1 \rangle \\ \zdiv{a+1}, & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: For an involution, Q is a subgroup of <r>, equal to <a-1> if b is in <a-1> and to ZDiv(a+1) otherwise; R\Q is described explicitly.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 4.8
nodes.statement: We proceed using Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} and applying Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}. Indeed, by Theorem \ref{thm:hqr} $\psi(Q)$ consists of the union of the two cosets $\langle a-1 \rangle$ and $-b + \langle a-1 \rangle$. These cosets are the same if $-b \in \langle a-1 \rangle$ (which means $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$) and then $\psi(Q) = \langle a - 1 \rangle \le \zdiv{a+1}$, or they are distinct and by Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols} part (1) there are only 2 cosets total so $\langle a - 1 \rangle \cup (-b+\langle a - 1 \rangle) = \zdiv{a+1}$. In either case, $Q$ is a subgroup of $\langle r \rangle$ and $\psi(Q)$ is as described in the statement of the corollary. Finally, the result about $R \setminus Q$ is immediate from equation \eqref{eqn:R}.

nodes.name: psi(Q) is almost always ZDiv(a+1)
nodes.statement: We note that due to Theorem \ref{thm:equivinvols}, $\psi(Q)$ given in Corollary \ref{cor:Q-is-ZDiv} is almost always $\zdiv{a+1}$ for involutions. The only instance where $\psi(Q)\ne \zdiv{a+1}$ occurs when $|\zdiv{a+1}/\langle a-1 \rangle|=2$ and $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$. We revisit $\theta_1=19x+18$ from Example \ref{autexamples}, which is an involution, noting that this is in fact a case where $b\in\langle a-1\rangle$. Recalling that $Q_1=\{1,r^{18}\}$, we see that $\psi (Q_1)$ is indeed isomorphic to $\langle a-1\rangle=\langle 18\rangle < \mathbb Z_{36}$. We also have that $R=R_1=\{1,r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{17},r^{18},r^{19},r^{21},\dots, r^{35}\}$, and thus $R_1\setminus Q_1=\{r,r^3,r^5,\dots,r^{35}\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: Our goal is to determine the size of $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|$ for all $n$. First, suppose that $n=p^r$ where $p$ is an odd prime and $r\geq 1$. Then, suppose $a\in\mathbb{Z}_{p^r}$ and that $a^2-1\equiv 0\pmod{p^r}$. Then we have that $(a+1)(a-1)\equiv 0$ (mod $p^r$) and so $(a+1)(a-1)=kp^r$ for some $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Since $p$ is an odd prime, it is clear that both $a+1$ and $a-1$ cannot divide $p^d$ for any $d\geq 1$ and so we have that $a+1=p^r$ or $a-1=p^r$. This implies that $a=1$ or $a=n-1$, thus $|\mathcal{R}_{p^r}^2|=2$. Next, it is clear that $|\mathcal{R}_2^2|=1$ and $|\mathcal{R}_4^2|=2$. Suppose that $n=2^m$ with $m\geq 3$. Next, suppose that $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n\setminus\{1,n-1\}$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). Since $n$ is even, we must have that $a$ is odd, so assume that $a=2k+1$ for some $0\leq k\leq 2^{m-1}$. Then $1\equiv a^2\equiv (2k+1)^2\equiv 4k^2+4k+1$ (mod $n$) so that $4k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^m$ for some $l\geq 1$. In particular, since $m\geq 3$, we have $k(k+1)=l\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $m$. Either $k$ or $k+1$ is odd and thus cannot divide $2^{m-2}$. \begin{enumerate} \item[] Case 1: $k$ is even. So $k=h\cdot 2^{m-2}$ for some $1\leq h\leq 2$ (since $k\leq 2^{m-1})$. We have counted the possibilities for $a_i$ above and so we can multiply these together to get all the possible choices for $a\in\mathbb{Z}_n$ with $a^2\equiv 1$ (mod $n$). In particular, we get $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^k$ if $m\in\{0,1\}$, $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2\cdot2^k$ if $m=2$ and $|\mathcal{R}_n^2|=2^2\cdot2^k$ if $m\geq 3$ as required.
